The test image shows a **microscopic view** of a fungal structure: a large, dark brown/black spherical sporangium with a collapsed columella and hyphae extending from it. This is characteristic of Rhizopus morphology.

Let me check reference images, starting with my top candidate and then spreading across other classes.

This Rhizopus reference (Bugwood 5369124) shows whitish mycelia with dark sporangia at lower magnification - same Bugwood series as the test image (5369127). The test image is clearly a higher magnification of one of those sporangia. Strong match.

Let me view references from 7 other classes to fulfill the budget requirement.
Gray Mold reference shows a macro stem lesion with fuzzy gray-brown sporulation. Not a match.
Alternaria stem canker reference shows macro stem lesions. Not a match.
Sclerotinia reference shows white cottony mycelium with grayish sclerotia on stem. Not a match.
Southern Blight shows white mycelium at stem base with soil. Not a match.
Anthracnose reference shows fruit rot with concentric rings. Not a match.

Late Blight reference shows microscopic Phytophthora sporangia - lemon/oval-shaped on branching sporangiophores. Very different from the test image's large spherical dark sporangium with collapsed columella.

Another Rhizopus reference (Bugwood 5369121, same series as test 5369127) showing heavy mycelial growth on stem. All images from the same Bugwood 536912x series documenting this Rhizopus soft rot case at different magnifications.

All 8 reference views used. The evidence is conclusive:

- The test image shows a **microscopic sporangium**: large, spherical, dark brown/black, with a visible collapsed columella and hyphae extending from it
- This matches **Rhizopus** morphology exactly: large spherical sporangia (~100-200 µm), columella, and sporangiophores
- The Bugwood ID (5369127) is from the same series as the Rhizopus_Soft_Rots references (5369121, 5369124)
- No other class shows this morphology. Late Blight sporangia are oval/lemon-shaped and much smaller. Gray Mold (Botrytis) conidia are grape-cluster-like. Alternaria spores are chain-forming and "hand grenade" shaped.
